stumbles.quote: I had assumed that e-means would mainly speed up training, and I had expected residual offset coding to be the win while index cells were a side note; the two uses came out the other way.
stumbles.why: It's unclear what 'the two uses came out the other way' means. Faster training was a stated result and residual coding gave a modest recall gain, so the reversal is confusing. The text also names three uses (training, residual coding, index cells), not two.

stumbles.quote: storing that 4,096-centroid table costs 126 bytes per vector
stumbles.why: A fixed centroid table amortized over 100,000 vectors is a small fraction of a byte per vector, or about 126 bytes only under unstated dimension and precision assumptions. The number is not derivable and looks inconsistent. The comparison to adding a second bit per dimension is also unquantified.
Passes are not defined or related to Lloyd iterations. The earlier '1.6 to 10.2 times sooner' speedup claim isn't reconciled with this.

stumbles.quote: so choosing between the two algorithms affects only how long index construction takes
stumbles.why: This conflicts with the earlier framing that e-means mainly changes cells and recall. It also ignores that the recall comparison is only reported within 0.005 on one dataset.

The baseline is unclear: it doesn't say whether 0.840 is plain 1-bit quantization, nor whether the table cost is included. The 90% neighbour capture figure is a different metric, which is also left undefined.

point: Using 4,096 e-means centroids as index cells captures 90% of true neighbours while scanning 0.56% of the corpus, far better than hash cells, and e-means gives the same recall as Lloyd's k-means with faster training.
